title: Blood Drive

jokes.text: Dwight impersonates a receptionist to intercept a salesman, pretending Michael isn't in — while Michael is clearly nearby
jokes.setup: A Techstar salesman arrives asking for Michael Scott; a 'receptionist' calmly says he's not in
jokes.punchline: It's Dwight doing the voice, and Michael is visibly present or nearby — the con is transparent and pointless
jokes.explanation: Works because it's quintessentially Dwight — overly committed to a pointless scheme. The joke builds slowly as we realize what's happening. Character-specific and earns points for the slow-burn reveal.

jokes.text: Dwight (as receptionist) describes his own job being replaced: 'Basically, 95% of my job. But I'd like to see a machine that puts out candy for everyone.' Salesman: 'Vending machine.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains that 95% of his job could be done by an automated phone system, then fantasizes about a machine that dispenses candy
jokes.punchline: The salesman flatly replies 'Vending machine,' instantly deflating Dwight's grandiose wishful thinking
jokes.explanation: Sharp economy — the salesman's two-word deadpan deflation is perfectly timed. Also contains the hidden absurdity that Dwight has described his own irrelevance while pretending to be someone else. Well-structured and funny.

jokes.text: Michael breaks his own cover and introduces himself to the salesman he sent Dwight to deflect: 'Michael Scott, manager. How are you?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has successfully stalled the salesman and is arranging for him to leave, having protected Michael from an unwanted meeting
jokes.punchline: Michael cheerfully blows the entire ruse by introducing himself, undermining everything Dwight just did
jokes.explanation: The payoff is classic Michael — his inability to stay out of any social situation destroys the plan. The callback structure is clean and the punchline requires zero explanation. High character integration: only Michael would do this.

jokes.text: Michael: 'That was funny. Let's go do it to somebody else.'
jokes.setup: They've just blown their own prank by Michael introducing himself; Dwight calls it funny
jokes.punchline: Michael enthusiastically agrees and immediately wants to repeat the scheme that just failed
jokes.explanation: A nice button on the cold open — both Michael and Dwight are completely oblivious to their failure. Character-consistent and efficiently delivered.

jokes.text: Michael on Valentine's Day decorations: 'Really shoving our faces in it this year.'
jokes.setup: Michael sees Valentine's Day decorations at the office; he's recently been separated from Holly
jokes.punchline: His bitterness is framed as if the decorations are a personal attack on him
jokes.explanation: Functional episode setup. The line is mildly amusing but not surprising — Michael's self-pity is well-established. Gets the episode's emotional premise rolling efficiently.

jokes.text: Michael to Kevin: 'It's been four months since I was with Holly. And she was way hotter than Stacy. So, if you think you're hurting...' Kevin: 'I can't even imagine.'
jokes.setup: Michael is consoling Kevin over his breakup with Stacy by commiserating about Holly
jokes.punchline: Michael turns it into a competition over whose ex was hotter, implying his pain is greater — and Kevin sincerely agrees with Michael's superiority
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration on both ends: Michael's narcissism hijacks what should be a comforting moment, and Kevin's earnest 'I can't even imagine' inadvertently validates the absurdity. Both characters come through perfectly.

jokes.text: Jim to Michael: 'You're only engaged once.' Michael: 'Present company excluded...' Jim: 'Really, Jim? On Cupid's birthday?'
jokes.setup: Pam says it's their first and only Valentine's Day as fiancees; Jim says 'you're only engaged once'
jokes.punchline: Michael pointedly notes Jim has been engaged before (to Carol), then catches himself and scolds Jim for bringing it up on Valentine's Day — even though Michael brought it up
jokes.explanation: Michael's double-take logic — raising a painful point and then blaming Jim for the mood — is classic Michael Scott misdirection. The 'Cupid's birthday' phrasing is a nice absurd touch.

jokes.text: Jim to Michael about calling him out on Valentine's Day: 'Really, Jim? On Cupid's birthday?'
jokes.setup: Jim calls out Michael's engagement hypocrisy
jokes.punchline: Michael reframes Valentine's Day as 'Cupid's birthday' — a factually incorrect and entirely Michaelian mythology that treats a commercialized holiday as a sacred birth anniversary
jokes.explanation: Short, sharp, quotable. Michael's misattribution of a holiday as a birthday — as if Cupid is a real person with a birth certificate — is a genuinely original comedic misfire that only Michael would make with complete conviction. Great economy.

jokes.text: Dwight reads his 'Valentine' aloud: 'Roses are red, violets are blue, it's time for your dental cleaning and maybe a check-up, too.'
jokes.setup: Dwight announces he received his first Valentine from a secret admirer
jokes.punchline: The 'Valentine' is a dental reminder postcard — Dwight has no idea and reads it with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is immaculate: the setup builds genuine audience anticipation, then the punchline is both surprising and completely logical. The humor layers: the rhyme scheme works, Dwight's obliviousness is perfectly in character (he would never recognize this as not a Valentine), and the subversion is maximally efficient. Quotable and rewatchable.

jokes.text: Michael moves Pam's flowers off her desk to the floor, claiming 'I wouldn't want them to fall' — a thin excuse to hide them from singles
jokes.setup: Pam has Valentine's Day flowers on her desk; Michael is on a crusade to protect singles from love displays
jokes.punchline: Michael's pretext for moving them is transparently false — 'I wouldn't want them to fall' — while he clearly just wants them hidden
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. The excuse is transparently bad, which is the joke. Serves the episode's running conflict more than it lands as a standalone bit.

jokes.text: Jim and/or Pam react to Dwight's Valentine with 'Look at those. How nice for you. Up there front and center, beautiful' — the condescending sweetness of not correcting him
jokes.setup: Dwight has just proudly displayed his 'Valentine' (dental reminder) and references flowers on display
jokes.punchline: Jim/Pam's over-the-top sincerity in praising what is clearly a dental flyer — choosing cruelty-by-kindness over correction
jokes.explanation: A functional secondary beat that extends joke #8's impact. The irony of praising a dental appointment card works, but it's more of a tag than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Just about everybody in this office is single right now, including me... everyone is experiencing an incredible amount of emotional pain. Especially me, because of my great capacity for emotion.'
jokes.setup: Michael is framing the Valentine's Day situation as a collective tragedy for the office
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to making it about his own superior suffering, citing his 'great capacity for emotion' as the reason he suffers most
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael: begins with genuine empathy and immediately cannibalize it into self-aggrandizement. The 'great capacity for emotion' line is both absurd and perfectly in character. Strong character integration keeps it above average.

jokes.text: Michael to Jim: 'The sexy looks between you and Pam, the general sexiness, the flowers... It's creating a bit of a hostile work environment.' Jim: 'It's so sexy it becomes hostile.'
jokes.setup: Michael confronts Jim about his relationship with Pam being upsetting to single people
jokes.punchline: Michael's framing of love as 'hostile' is absurd; Jim's deadpan repeat of Michael's logic highlights how ridiculous it is
jokes.explanation: Jim's reflexive echo of Michael's logic is a good straight-man move — he's not correcting Michael, just reflecting the absurdity back. The legal framing of 'hostile work environment' for being too in love is a clever inversion.

jokes.text: 'A lonely hearts convention this afternoon. Singles only. Deal with it, Pam!'
jokes.setup: Michael is announcing his singles party as a counter to Jim and Pam's couplehood
jokes.punchline: He punctuates the announcement with 'Deal with it, Pam!' — a nonsensical victory cry directed at someone who has nothing to lose from this party
jokes.explanation: The 'Deal with it, Pam' is the punchline — Michael declaring victory over Pam by having a singles party she literally doesn't care about. Solid character beat.

jokes.text: Dwight at blood drive: 'I've trained my major blood vessels to retract into my body on command. Also, I can retract my penis up into itself.'
jokes.setup: A nurse is having trouble finding a vein in Dwight's arm
jokes.punchline: Dwight claims he has trained his veins to hide — then escalates to the non-sequitur claim that he can also retract his penis
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The first claim (trained blood vessels) is already absurdist Dwight, but the escalation to penile retraction is the masterstroke. It's completely unprompted, delivered with total sincerity, and is maximally specific and weird. Quintessentially Dwight — he thinks this is useful information to share with a medical professional. High originality, exceptional character integration, and the escalation structure is flawless. A near-legendary Dwight moment.

jokes.text: Michael at the blood drive sees the needle: 'That's a big needle.' Nurse: 'You're gonna need to lie down over here.' Michael: 'I can't talk right now. I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been talking about giving blood as 'the gift of everlasting life' and the 'transfer of my bodily fluids'
jokes.punchline: He sees the needle and immediately shuts down, going from grandiose to terrified in one beat
jokes.explanation: A reliable comedic beat — the blowhard deflated by reality. Efficient and character-appropriate, though not particularly original. The 'I can't talk right now' polite shutdown is a nice specific touch.

jokes.text: Man at blood drive: 'When I get nervous I sort of clam up.' Woman: 'That's fine.' Man: 'It's better for me just to be quiet.' Woman: 'You're actually talking a lot.'
jokes.setup: A nervous man tells the woman next to him that when he's nervous, he clams up and goes quiet
jokes.punchline: She points out he's been talking continuously, directly contradicting his self-description
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical irony. The joke is structurally perfect — he describes his own behavior wrong in the act of doing the behavior. Slightly lower character integration since these are essentially strangers/unnamed characters. The 'Sorry, it's the other thing I do' callback within the same exchange adds a nice layer.

jokes.text: Man: 'Sorry, it's the other thing I do when I get really nervous.' (talking too much, contradicting his claim of going quiet)
jokes.setup: He just said he clams up when nervous; she pointed out he's talking a lot
jokes.punchline: He reframes the talking as 'the other thing I do' — admitting nervousness manifests in two opposite ways and acknowledging both without embarrassment
jokes.explanation: A nice capper to the blood drive meet-cute exchange. The self-contradiction explained as 'the other thing' is endearing and specific. Good economy.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I feel like a human juice box.'
jokes.setup: Michael is lying down giving blood, needle in arm
jokes.punchline: He describes the sensation with the specific, childlike metaphor of a 'juice box'
jokes.explanation: Four words of maximum efficiency. The 'juice box' framing is childlike and specific — exactly how Michael would think of it. It's unexpectedly vivid and the specificity of 'juice box' over, say, 'juice carton' or 'blood bag' makes it funnier. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Hawaiian Blood Punch.' Oscar: 'That's gross.' Kevin: 'Type O-cean Spray.'
jokes.setup: Michael says he feels like a human juice box; the office riffs on blood-themed juice brand names
jokes.punchline: 'Type O-cean Spray' — a pun combining blood type (Type O) with Ocean Spray cranberry juice brand
jokes.explanation: The 'Type O-cean Spray' pun is genuinely clever — it layers blood type nomenclature with the brand name seamlessly. 'Hawaiian Blood Punch' is a warm-up, but 'Type O-cean Spray' earns the laugh. Oscar's 'That's gross' reaction beats are good rhythm. The wordplay is tight and earns its placement.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'Why don't you guys come and have lunch with Bob and me? We'll take all afternoon. Michael is terrified of Bob.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis invites Jim and Pam to lunch as if it's a favor
jokes.punchline: She casually drops that Michael is 'terrified of Bob' as a benefit/selling point, which is both funny and completely true to form
jokes.explanation: The matter-of-fact delivery of 'Michael is terrified of Bob' as a perk is a nice character beat. Phyllis weaponizing her intimidating husband is consistent with her character's quiet power. Efficient.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I have a lot of work to do this afternoon. Those mines aren't gonna sweep themselves.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis has invited Jim and Pam to lunch; Jim is considering whether to accept
jokes.punchline: Jim makes up a completely absurd fake excuse ('mine sweeping') delivered with utter sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim deadpan. The joke works on multiple levels: the excuse is absurd (paper salesmen don't sweep mines), the 'those mines aren't gonna sweep themselves' construction mimics real workplace logic, and it's delivered completely straight. Highly economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Kevin (presumably after his elaborate excuse about mine-sweeping) simply says 'We're in.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has just given a complicated excuse about mine-sweeping to avoid the lunch
jokes.punchline: Immediate reversal — 'We're in' — abandoning the excuse without comment
jokes.explanation: The callback punchline on Kevin's mine-sweeping joke. The complete abandonment of his elaborate excuse without any explanation is a perfect tag. Maximum economy — two words erase everything he just said.

jokes.text: Man at blood drive: 'I looked at the bag. I looked straight at the bag.' (referring to his blood bag)
jokes.setup: The man is trying not to look at his blood bag while giving blood
jokes.punchline: He confesses with quiet horror that he made direct eye contact with his own blood bag — delivered as a genuine crisis
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'I looked straight at the bag' and the solemnity with which it's delivered carry the joke. Relatable cringe anxiety played well.

jokes.text: Woman tries to distract him: 'Bags.' Man: 'What? That was bad.' Woman: 'A hat.' Man: 'A hat with no blood in it.' Woman: 'That is full of soup.'
jokes.setup: She's trying to distract him from the blood bag by naming random objects
jokes.punchline: Her 'bags' distraction is immediately the worst possible word; she recovers with 'a hat' but he corrects it to 'a hat with no blood in it'; she then says 'that is full of soup' — an absurd non-sequitur that lands perfectly
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalating absurdism. 'Bags' is the wrong word — good. 'A hat' recovers — nice. 'A hat with no blood in it' — the modification reveals his anxiety. 'That is full of soup' — a complete non-sequitur that somehow makes perfect sense in the logic of the scene. The escalation is expertly paced and the soup line is genuinely surprising. One of the episode's most creative comedic constructions.

jokes.text: Woman says 'You're cute' to the nervous man; then immediately: 'You're done.'
jokes.setup: The two have been bonding awkwardly over his blood-giving anxiety
jokes.punchline: 'You're cute' sounds like a romantic moment — immediately undercut by 'You're done' (referring to giving blood), deflating the romantic charge
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection — 'You're cute' sets a romantic expectation, 'You're done' is a procedural pivot. The joke is efficient and the timing between the two statements does the work. The ambiguity of whether 'you're cute' was sincere adds a layer.

jokes.text: Man after blood draw: 'I was so nervous about this I don't think I ate for three days.' Then faints.
jokes.setup: He's just relieved it's over and declares he was so nervous he didn't eat
jokes.punchline: Fainting immediately after — the three days without eating contributed to passing out, making the oversharing self-report the cause of the physical gag
jokes.explanation: The faint is telegraphed by the three days without food — the setup earns the payoff. Standard physical comedy but the cause-and-effect logic is satisfying.

jokes.text: Man regaining consciousness: 'How long was I out?'
jokes.setup: He just fainted at the blood drive
jokes.punchline: His first words upon waking are the clichéd 'how long was I out' — performed with complete earnestness as if he's a war hero, not someone who passed out giving blood
jokes.explanation: The cliché is deployed sincerely, which makes it mildly funny. The gap between the gravitas of the line and the mundane cause (donating blood) is the joke. Functional but not especially creative.

jokes.text: Michael wakes up from fainting, immediately asks the waitress where 'the lady' went — he's conflated the blood drive with a restaurant
jokes.setup: Michael has fainted at the blood drive; upon waking, he's disoriented
jokes.punchline: He calls out to a 'waitress' and asks where the woman went — treating the blood drive as if it were a romantic restaurant encounter
jokes.explanation: The 'waitress' misidentification reveals how Michael has romanticized the blood drive encounter. It's a good character beat — Michael's tendency to narrative-ize his life leads him to see a blood drive as a candlelit dinner.

jokes.text: Dwight tears the wings off a paper Cupid decoration, leaving just the baby: 'Now it's just a stupid baby.'
jokes.setup: Michael has enlisted Dwight to help decorate for the singles party; Dwight is modifying Valentine's decorations
jokes.punchline: After removing wings from a Cupid figure, Dwight announces with flat satisfaction 'Now it's just a stupid baby' — as if this is an improvement
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect five-word joke. The logic is Dwight's alone — de-winged Cupid IS technically just a baby, and his contemptuous satisfaction in identifying this is deeply in character. 'Stupid baby' has exactly the right dismissive energy. Economy is exceptional, character integration is near-perfect, and it's extremely quotable. One of the episode's top three jokes.

jokes.text: Phyllis about working with Michael, Dwight, and Andy: 'I honestly don't know how you can work with this jack-ass and that other jack-ass and that new jack-ass.'
jokes.setup: Bob Vance is commenting on Jim's coworkers
jokes.punchline: The triple 'jack-ass' with spatial descriptors ('this,' 'that other,' 'that new') is both funny for its bluntness and the escalating specificity of how many jack-asses there are
jokes.explanation: Bob Vance's blunt plainspokenness is his character trait, and the escalating trio of jackasses lands. Not particularly crafted but the delivery and specificity carry it.

jokes.text: Jim: 'He's talking about Michael, Dwight and Andy.' Phyllis: 'I understood.'
jokes.setup: Bob Vance has just called out 'this jack-ass and that other jack-ass and that new jack-ass'
jokes.punchline: Jim helpfully clarifies to the camera who the three jackasses are; Phyllis flatly says 'I understood' — she didn't need the translation
jokes.explanation: Phyllis's 'I understood' is a perfect two-word deflation of Jim's unnecessary narration. The mockumentary format makes Jim's aside natural, and Phyllis shutting it down is a nice subversion of who the straight man is in this scene.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Alone but together. No flowers for us. Relationships? We don't need no stinkin' relationships.'
jokes.setup: Michael is rallying the singles group at their Valentine's lunch
jokes.punchline: The 'We don't need no stinkin' relationships' is a parody of the famous 'Badges? We don't need no stinkin' badges!' — deployed by Michael who clearly desperately needs a relationship
jokes.explanation: The pop culture reference is recognizable but the twist isn't particularly clever — it's a straight substitution without much added value. The irony of Michael saying it is the real joke, which is strong, but the vehicle is mediocre.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Kelly, what about Ryan? He treated you pretty terribly...' Kelly: 'His heart was in the right place.' Michael: 'But now his heart is in Thailand... Along with the rest of his body, having random sex.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to get Kelly to share her worst breakup story about Ryan
jokes.punchline: He pivots Kelly's charitable 'his heart was in the right place' into a specific (and cruel) image of Ryan in Thailand having random sex
jokes.explanation: The wordplay on 'heart in the right place' → 'heart in Thailand' is sharp and the 'having random sex' specificity is darkly funny. Character-appropriate for Michael (oblivious to how hurtful this is to Kelly) and the callback to Ryan's Season 4/5 arc gives it extra bite for regular viewers.

jokes.text: Michael tries to get Oscar to share a story: 'I'm sure whatever you did wasn't your fault.' Oscar declines. Awkward silence and Michael moves on.
jokes.setup: Michael is going around the table soliciting worst breakup stories; he pauses on Oscar
jokes.punchline: Oscar's firm 'I'm sure' decline, followed by Michael's preemptive absolution ('whatever you did wasn't your fault') and then abrupt pivot, implies Oscar has something he's not sharing — the unspoken is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is the conspicuous absence — Oscar's pointed refusal and Michael's quick pivot suggest a secret. Subtle cringe comedy that works better on rewatch when you might know more about Oscar's storyline. Understated.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Everyone here who's bowled a 280, please raise your hand.' (pause) 'Now everyone here who's bowled under 70 raise their hand.'
jokes.setup: Michael transitions the group away from relationship talk with a non-sequitur bowling question
jokes.punchline: The follow-up question — who bowled under 70 — implies he's about to call someone out for terrible bowling, immediately reversing the initial direction
jokes.explanation: A good topic pivot that also sets up the Jim bowling story. The gap between 280 and sub-70 is itself funny — these are wildly different skill levels being invoked in the same breath.

jokes.text: Bob Vance reveals Jim bowled five frames with a pink sparkly ball 'until a little girl had to ask for her ball back.' Jim: 'That girl must have had monstrous hands because the holes fit.'
jokes.setup: Bob calls Jim out for bowling with a child's ball
jokes.punchline: Jim's defense — that the girl must have had monstrous hands since the holes fit — is technically logical but practically absurd, and he delivers it with total commitment
jokes.explanation: Jim's deadpan defense is excellent — he doesn't deny any of it, just constructs an absurd but logically structured counter-argument. 'Monstrous hands' is the specific, weird image that sells it. Bob immediately calling out his 'dainty fingers' is a good double-punch.

jokes.text: Bob Vance: 'You could model ladies' jewelry.' Jim: 'Nobody asked, Bob.'
jokes.setup: Bob is mocking Jim's 'little dainty fingers' after the bowling ball story
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'Nobody asked, Bob' is a perfect straight-man reaction — defensive but unable to deny it, suggesting the ladies' jewelry modeling is accurate
jokes.explanation: 'Nobody asked, Bob' is a great reaction line — it's the kind of defeated, specific retort that sounds real. Jim using Bob's name in the dismissal adds formality that contrasts with the childishness of the argument. Economical and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Woman at singles party shares that a man told her he wasn't gay — then was spotted in a gay bar in Kansas City. Kevin: 'Then it's a happy ending, because he was gay. You should call him.'
jokes.setup: A woman shares a sad story about a man who claimed he wasn't gay but was seen in a gay bar
jokes.punchline: Kevin interprets the gay bar revelation as a 'happy ending' and advises calling him — utterly missing the point of why this was a painful rejection
jokes.explanation: Kevin's misunderstanding is perfect Kevin — his logic is internally consistent but emotionally tone-deaf. 'He was gay, so he wasn't rejecting you personally' is actually Kevin's attempt at comfort, which makes it both funny and a little sweet. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'My worst breakup was actually two breakups. Two different men. I was in love with both of them, and when things went bad, they had a duel over me.'
jokes.setup: The group is sharing worst breakup stories; Meredith takes her turn
jokes.punchline: Meredith reveals she was the subject of an actual duel — a completely improbable, romantic-novel scenario from a character known for chaotic, undignified life choices
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes entirely from the gap between Meredith's character (slovenly, chaotic, unlucky) and the romantic grandeur of 'they had a duel over me.' The deadpan delivery makes it even better. The reveal that it was not Dwight and Andy (as the audience might expect) but two different Johns is a nice misdirection.

jokes.text: After Meredith says two men dueled over her, Michael's reaction: 'Dwight and Andy. We were here.' — then realizes it was years ago with different men
jokes.setup: Meredith reveals men dueled over her; Michael instinctively assumes it was Dwight and Andy (who actually did duel over Angela)
jokes.punchline: Michael connects it to the known Dwight/Andy duel, but this is a completely different duel — implying multiple duels have occurred in the orbit of this office
jokes.explanation: Strong callback for regular viewers — Michael's assumption that any duel must involve Dwight and Andy is both in-character and a knowing wink to the show's lore. The revelation that duels are apparently common enough to generate confusion is itself a joke.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Where's Andy?' Oscar: 'He's on one of his honeymoons.' Michael: 'What?' Oscar: 'He made non-refundable deposits on his honeymoons, so he's knockin' 'em off one at a time. I think today he's hot air ballooning, and later he's got a couples' massage.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks where Andy is; Oscar explains
jokes.punchline: Andy, having been jilted by Angela, is systematically completing his pre-booked honeymoon activities alone — hot air ballooning and a couples' massage, solo
jokes.explanation: The 'knockin' 'em off one at a time' framing treats romantic catastrophe like a to-do list, which is both sad and deeply funny. The specificity of 'couples' massage' (alone) and hot air ballooning is perfectly chosen — activities that are maximally awkward to do solo. Strong character integration (this is absolutely what Andy would do) and high originality.

jokes.text: Kevin's worst breakup story: 'I said, "My god. I think the Eagles could clinch the N.F.C. East." And she said... "We're done."'
jokes.setup: Kevin is sharing his worst breakup story with Stacy
jokes.punchline: Kevin's entire account of the breakup is that he mentioned the Eagles might clinch the NFC East — with zero self-awareness about how this might have been the last straw in a longer relationship
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is near-perfect: Kevin builds up to sharing his 'worst breakup,' treats the Eagles comment as the complete and sufficient explanation, and delivers Stacy's 'We're done' with the same gravity as if it were the inciting incident rather than the inevitable conclusion of something much longer. The joke trusts the audience to fill in years of context. The dramatic pause before 'We're done' is excellent structure. Character integration is exceptional — only Kevin would tell this story this way.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I look around and I see all these beautiful people who are alone on Valentine's.' Then: 'There has to be a way to get all these lonely people together.' Dwight: 'A net? A giant net?'
jokes.setup: Michael is musing about connecting lonely singles in the office park
jokes.punchline: Dwight's first instinct is a giant net — as if the singles need to be caught like animals
jokes.explanation: 'A net? A giant net?' is peak Dwight. His immediate conceptual leap from 'get people together' to 'net them like prey' is deranged and perfect. The double take ('A net?... A giant net?') as if he's refining his solution makes it even better. High character integration and economy — it's just five words but it's completely Dwight.

jokes.text: Dwight on a singles mixer: 'Terrible idea. Old-fashioned meat market. Lonely people mixing with one another? Breeding? Creating an even lonelier generation?'
jokes.setup: Michael proposes a mixer for singles in the office park
jokes.punchline: Dwight's objection escalates to eugenics-adjacent concerns about 'lonely people breeding' and the existential horror of a 'lonelier generation'
jokes.explanation: Dwight's concern about the genetic implications of lonely people reproducing is brilliantly unhinged. The escalation from 'bad idea' to 'you're not allowing natural selection to do its work' is a fast, dark climb. Only Dwight would frame a Valentine's Day mixer as a threat to species fitness.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You're not allowing natural selection to do its work. Like the guy who invented the seat belt.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is arguing against Michael's singles mixer by invoking natural selection
jokes.punchline: He compares Michael to the inventor of the seat belt — framing safety devices as obstacles to natural selection — revealing his deeply anti-humanitarian worldview with casual conviction
jokes.explanation: The seat belt line is the sharpest beat in this sequence. It takes Dwight's natural selection argument to its logical but absurd extreme — he genuinely believes seat belts are a problem. The joke is funny because the logic is internally consistent even as it's morally horrifying. High originality and near-perfect character integration. A standout Dwight moment.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'I am going to be Cupid, and I am going to shoot my sparrow at unsuspecting victims... "I'm in love! I was hit by Cupid's sparrow." Funny little bird, but he gets the job done.'
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining his plan to play matchmaker
jokes.punchline: He calls Cupid's arrow a 'sparrow' — either a malapropism or deliberate substitution — and defends the bird with 'funny little bird, but he gets the job done'
jokes.explanation: The arrow-to-sparrow substitution is classically Michael — he's confident in the mythology he's invented. The defensive 'funny little bird, but he gets the job done' is the best part, as he preemptively defends his fictional bird against criticism. Strong Michael voice throughout.

jokes.text: Michael spots an attractive woman in the office park: 'Babe alert! I'm Michael Scott. Welcome to our little shindig.' Then immediately assigns her to Kevin: 'For you, we have one of our top people. Kevin Malone.'
jokes.setup: Michael is playing Cupid at his singles mixer
jokes.punchline: Michael greets an attractive woman enthusiastically — then immediately pawns her off on Kevin, designating him a 'top person' in a way that's completely unconvincing
jokes.explanation: 'Babe alert' as an announcement, combined with the immediate re-gift to Kevin, is good Michael. The 'one of our top people' framing for Kevin is delightful in its transparent dishonesty.

jokes.text: Michael pushes Kevin toward Lynn: 'So run with the ball. Run with it, Kev.' Kevin's approach: 'Where are you from?' Lynn: 'I'm from here.' (long pause) Michael: 'He only gets better.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has been set up with Lynn; Michael is coaching from the sidelines
jokes.punchline: Kevin's entire opening is 'Where are you from?' followed by silence. Michael's cover line — 'He only gets better' — is both reassuring and deeply alarming
jokes.explanation: 'He only gets better' is a perfect comedy line in context — it's Michael's spin, it implies this IS the floor, and it inadvertently damns Kevin. The awkward silence after Lynn's one-word answer does heavy comedic lifting.

jokes.text: Kevin to Lynn: 'I can untie any knot. I'm serious. Name a knot, any knot. Go ahead.' Lynn: 'I believe you.' Kevin: 'You shouldn't believe everything you hear. In fact, there are many knots that I cannot untie.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is trying to impress Lynn with his conversation skills
jokes.punchline: Kevin makes a bold claim about knot untying, she accepts it — and he immediately recants, confessing the claim was false
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is masterful: Kevin makes an extravagant brag, she neutralizes it by simply believing him (removing his ability to demonstrate the skill), and he responds by spontaneously confessing he was lying — abandoning the bluff entirely when there's no need to. 'There are many knots that I cannot untie' is an extraordinary specific retreat. This is deeply Kevin: unable to maintain even a low-stakes lie. High originality, exceptional structure, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight to Lynn: 'Where does a woman as charming as yourself find herself employed on a day such as today?' Lynn: 'I work at a place that does catalogs for community colleges and small businesses.' Dwight: 'You must use a lot of paper.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is attempting social conversation at the mixer
jokes.punchline: His grandiose romantic opener leads directly to a paper sales pitch — the instant business pivot reveals he has no genuine social mode
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Dwight's ornate opener ('a woman as charming as yourself on a day such as today') and the immediate pivot to 'you must use a lot of paper' is perfectly timed. His salesmanship is deeper than his humanity. Strong character integration — the joke works because Dwight cannot separate his identity from Dunder Mifflin.

jokes.text: Dwight uses his opening line on a woman at the mixer: 'Where does a woman as charming as yourself find herself employed on a day such as today?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is attempting to chat up a woman at the mixer using what he thinks is a suave opening
jokes.punchline: The line is painfully formal and archaic ('a day such as today,' 'find herself employed') — not actually a bad pickup line by Dwight standards, which makes it cringe-funny rather than catastrophically wrong
jokes.explanation: The formality of Dwight's approach is perfectly in character — he treats flirtation as a formal interview. The joke is mild: it's not catastrophically bad, just deeply Dwight. Works as a character beat but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Pam: 'What's the rule about eating when people are in the bathroom?' Jim: 'I think if you ordered hot food, you're allowed to eat.' Pam: 'Damn.' Then: 'They've been in there for like ten minutes.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis and Bob Vance have both gone to the bathroom, leaving Jim and Pam alone at the lunch table with hot food
jokes.punchline: The etiquette debate over bathroom-absence eating, combined with Pam's 'Damn' of defeated compliance, is relatable and the ten minutes detail escalates the awkwardness
jokes.explanation: Relatable observational comedy about dining etiquette. The 'ten minutes' escalation hints at something happening in the bathroom — the joke is understated and depends on implication. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Unnamed man at mixer to the woman he met: 'The circle drive-in, they show old movies. It's really cool. I used to go there with my fiancee. Before she left me. I mean, before I left her.' (pause) 'She left me.'
jokes.setup: The man from the blood drive is attempting to charm the woman with a date idea
jokes.punchline: His date suggestion collapses into a confession of being left by his fiancee — he tries to save face ('I left her'), fails, and is forced to admit the truth ('She left me.') in a perfectly timed three-beat
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes purely on structure. The three-beat is perfectly constructed: romantic idea → tragic context → face-saving lie → immediate honest retraction. 'She left me.' lands as both funny and genuinely poignant. The pause between 'I left her' and 'She left me' is where the joke lives — his inability to maintain even a small lie makes the moment human. Economy is exceptional: the whole arc takes about ten seconds of dialogue.

jokes.text: Michael: 'So Erik, you mentioned before that you are in tool and dye repair.' Michael: 'Meredith recently had a total hysterectomy. So that's sort of a repair.'
jokes.setup: Michael is attempting to play matchmaker between Erik (tool and die repair) and Meredith
jokes.punchline: He equates tool-and-die repair with Meredith's hysterectomy — framing a gynecological procedure as a professional connection point
jokes.explanation: The hysterectomy-as-repair logic is absurdist and grotesque in just the right way. Michael's obliviousness to why this is inappropriate is perfectly in character. The 'so that's sort of a repair' confidence sells it.

jokes.text: Jim notices Michael keeps glancing at the door; Michael explains he met a woman giving blood and their blood bags touched: 'I think our blood bags touched.'
jokes.setup: Jim calls out Michael's behavior of watching the front door
jokes.punchline: Michael's romanticization of the blood drive encounter culminates in 'our blood bags touched' as if it were a first kiss
jokes.explanation: 'Our blood bags touched' as a romantic milestone is perfect Michael. He has genuinely constructed a love story around two intravenous bags making incidental contact. The sincerity makes it both funny and oddly touching. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jim: 'When you were giving blood? That is so romantic.' Michael dismisses it: 'It's not a big deal, really.' Jim: 'This is like a modern-day enchanted. It's like a fairy tale.' Michael: 'Not likely. 3 billion women on the planet, most of them in Asia, so the numbers just don't add up.'
jokes.setup: Jim is being sincerely enthusiastic about Michael's blood drive romance; Michael is trying to downplay it
jokes.punchline: Michael deflates his own romantic hope with geographic probability statistics — '3 billion women on the planet, most of them in Asia, so the numbers just don't add up' — a deeply weird way to convince yourself a relationship is unlikely
jokes.explanation: The 'most of them in Asia' pivot is the unexpected specific detail that elevates this from a generic self-deprecation to a genuine Michael Scott joke. His statistical logic is technically correct and practically meaningless. The dismissal of his own odds using global demographics is both original and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Here they come.' (pause) 'No, just kidding.'
jokes.setup: Michael is anxiously watching the door for Lynn to appear
jokes.punchline: Jim fakes a sighting of Lynn to mess with Michael, then immediately admits he's joking
jokes.explanation: A standard Jim prank beat. Functional and in-character but minimal craft. The quick admission 'No, just kidding' removes some of the cringe potential. Ordinary.

jokes.text: Pam and Jim debate covering food: 'Just cover it with the broccoli.' Jim: 'Great, I have to cover it. Do you think they dined and dashed?' Pam: 'They didn't dine.' Jim: 'Maybe they just dashed.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis and Bob have been gone even longer; Jim and Pam are covering untouched food
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'They didn't dine' / Jim's 'Maybe they just dashed' — playing on the phrase 'dine and dash' to note Phyllis and Bob haven't eaten, only departed
jokes.explanation: The wordplay on 'dine and dash' is well-constructed — parsing out the two components and applying them separately. Pam and Jim's banter is comfortable and the implication that Phyllis and Bob are in the bathroom together doing something other than eating is the underlying cringe.

jokes.text: Michael is at his singles party; it appears to be just him alone in the conference room with no guests. 'Is this the party?'
jokes.setup: Michael organized a singles mixer in the office park and has been enthusiastically promoting it
jokes.punchline: The party appears to be just Michael alone (or nearly so) — the shot of the empty/near-empty conference room contrasts with his big promotional energy
jokes.explanation: The visual joke of a nearly empty party after all of Michael's grandiose planning is a reliable sitcom beat. Works well here because of the specific investment he's made in this event. The question 'Is this the party?' from a visitor underscores the deflation.

jokes.text: Bob: 'You didn't eat much there, Jimbo.' Jim: 'Initially I did.' Bob: 'Want some meat?' Jim: 'Sure. Little piece.' Bob: 'No mushroom, though.' Jim: 'I forgot.'
jokes.setup: Back at the restaurant after the Phyllis/Bob bathroom incident; Jim is visibly off his appetite
jokes.punchline: Bob's casual food offers and Jim's terse responses reveal Jim is still processing the bathroom revelation — 'I forgot' about the mushroom implies distraction-by-trauma
jokes.explanation: The aftermath joke — Jim's lost appetite as the continuing fallout of the bathroom incident. 'I forgot' about the mushroom is a nice understated callback. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Blood drive man apologizes to Lynn at the party: 'I get very nervous talking to pretty girls. Seriously. Feel how sweaty my hand is.' She feels it: 'That's really sweaty.'
jokes.setup: The man is trying to apologize for blurting out his fiancee story
jokes.punchline: He confesses nervousness, then invites her to physically verify it by touching his sweaty hand — which she does, confirming the sweatiness
jokes.explanation: The invitation to touch the sweaty hand is the joke — it's an overshare and a physical imposition at once. Her matter-of-fact confirmation 'That's really sweaty' rather than recoiling is a good character choice that makes it endearing. The cringe is softened by the warmth.

jokes.text: Dwight tries to get Lynn to commit to paper order before she leaves the party: 'Before you go, I'd just love to get a firm commitment on this. Maybe sign?' Lynn: 'We already have a paper supplier.' Dwight: 'Thanks for wasting my time tonight. Idiot.'
jokes.setup: Lynn is leaving; Dwight moves to close a paper sale
jokes.punchline: Lynn reveals they have a supplier; Dwight immediately and personally insults her — 'Thanks for wasting my time tonight. Idiot.' — as if the entire mixer was a sales call
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top three jokes. 'Thanks for wasting my time tonight. Idiot.' is a perfect Dwight line in every dimension: it's delivered with utter sincerity, it reveals that Dwight attended this romantic mixer purely as a sales opportunity, and his genuine offense at being unable to close is completely in character. The word 'Idiot' alone, dropped at the end, is exceptional comedic economy. Near-perfect character integration — this joke could ONLY be Dwight.

jokes.text: After Dwight insults Lynn and she walks away: Dwight says quietly to himself or the camera: 'You don't deserve her.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just called Lynn an idiot for not buying paper
jokes.punchline: He pivots to a dignified chivalric gesture — 'You don't deserve her' — as if he was always on Kevin's side, not his own commercial interests
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the previous joke. Having just insulted Lynn for not buying paper, Dwight's pivot to protective outrage on Kevin's behalf — 'You don't deserve her' — is unexpected and rich with Dwight's particular moral code. It's a great example of The Office's ability to make Dwight genuinely charming right after making him terrible.

jokes.text: Michael talking head about Holly: 'Sometimes it's not about whether Cinderella gets her slipper back, but it's about the fact that the prince even picked up the slipper at all. There's a lot of princesses out there. They have all different sizes and shapes of feet. And hands.'
jokes.setup: Michael reflects emotionally on his Holly situation and the glove woman
jokes.punchline: A sincere metaphor about Cinderella slowly degrades into Michael specifying that princesses have different-sized feet 'and hands' — the addition of 'and hands' being a completely unnecessary and odd extension that reveals Michael's inability to land an emotional moment cleanly
jokes.explanation: The 'and hands' is the genius move — Michael's metaphor was almost profound, and the awkward addition of hands (returning to the glove story) undercuts the moment perfectly. It's both funny and a little sad, which is The Office at its best. Strong character integration — Michael cannot quite achieve the emotional depth he's reaching for.

jokes.text: Michael asks a woman at a cookie table for a cookie: 'I gave blood earlier and I'm still feeling woozy.' Woman: 'Of course.' Second person: 'That's weird. You got a cotton ball and tape and we've been using band-aids.' Michael: 'I feel so woozy. I just...' Other person: 'It's band-aids.' Michael: 'Damn.'
jokes.setup: Michael uses the blood donation as an excuse to get a free cookie; someone notices his cotton-ball bandage (better treatment than others got) rather than a band-aid
jokes.punchline: Michael is caught getting premium post-donation care (cotton ball and tape vs. regular band-aids) — his VIP treatment at the blood drive is exposed at the most inopportune moment, undermining his cookie sympathy play
jokes.explanation: A nice late-episode callback. Michael's premium bandaging (cotton ball and tape, usually reserved for needle-phobic fainters) is exposed right as he's playing the sympathy card. The 'Damn.' at the end is a perfectly Michael deflation — he's been caught being a fraud but still got the cookie, so the loss is ambiguous.

tmdb_overview: A mystery woman at the office blood drive catches Michael's eye. Dwight and Kevin both find women at the "Lonely Hearts Party," while Jim and Pam are forced to leave because of PDAs—so they have lunch with Phyllis and Bob.
